The paper proposes an automatic workflow for assessing damage on gas turbine blades using deep learning on borescope video feeds.
The workflow uses a Mask R-CNN neural network with PointRend for instance segmentation to detect and classify different types of blade damage.
The workflow can detect and classify five types of blade damage: casing, compressor-rotor, surface-damage, material-separation, and material-deformation.

The blade tracking algorithm matches blades between adjacent frames based on the Euclidean distance between the centers of their bounding boxes, assuming blades do not move significantly between frames.
Damage is quantified for each blade as a fraction of the projected area of the blade visible in that frame.
A post-processing step applies a high-pass filter and masked erosion to highlight small surface damage features that may have been missed by the neural network.
The Mask R-CNN network was trained on 89 manually labeled images and evaluated on 15 test images.
The mean average precision (mAP) and mean matched IoU were used as evaluation metrics, showing improved performance after 2000 training iterations.
The workflow was able to track individual blades across the video frames and provide detailed damage statistics for each blade.
The manual labeling process used to generate training data may introduce human biases, and the training dataset size is small compared to common computer vision benchmarks.
Incorporating factors beyond just the area/size of damage, such as the location of damage, could provide a more comprehensive assessment.
The blade tracking algorithm would need to be extended for cases where the borescope camera is non-stationary during inspection.

The authors find that the classification of defects on gas turbine blades presented from various sources is inconsistent and sometimes incomplete, leading to variability in practices among different parties.
Borescope imaging is a popular technique that allows an inspector to probe the interior of an engine with minimal disassembly.
The cost of repairing damage caused by foreign object debris (FOD) can exceed $1 million for a single overhaul operation per engine, exceeding 20% of the engine's list price.
